> Archived exploratory analysis. The [revised benchmark](../benchmark/README.md) uses a different statistical and scoring protocol.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6.4, fig.height = 3.1, dpi = 300)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 9) +
            theme(axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.4),
                  axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.4),
                  legend.key.size = unit(0.35, "cm")))

rd <- function(f) if (file.exists(f)) read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                                              check.names = FALSE) else NULL
bench  <- rd("../benchmark/scores/benchmark_summary.csv")
abl    <- rd("../benchmark/scores/ablation_summary.csv")
recall <- rd("../benchmark/scores/pathway_recall.csv")
gt     <- read.csv("../benchmark/ground_truth.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                   check.names = FALSE)

ora <- recall[recall$arm == "ORA_only", ]
llm <- recall[recall$arm == "LLM", ]
MODELS  <- c("deepseek-flash", "deepseek-v4-pro")
N_DS    <- nrow(gt)
N_CELLS <- N_DS * length(MODELS)
N_DONE  <- nrow(bench)

f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f\\%%", 100 * x)

ora5  <- mean(ora$hit_at_5);  ora10 <- mean(ora$hit_at_10)
ora5n <- sum(ora$hit_at_5);   ora10n <- sum(ora$hit_at_10)
rec_mean <- mean(bench$recovery_keyword)
rec_min  <- min(bench$recovery_keyword); rec_max <- max(bench$recovery_keyword)
cost_med <- median(bench$cost_usd);      cost_max <- max(bench$cost_usd)
cost_tot <- sum(bench$cost_usd)
hal_max  <- max(bench$hallucination_rate)
fs_off <- tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$few_shot, mean)[1]
fs_on  <- tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$few_shot, mean)[2]
fs_tok <- tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, abl$few_shot, mean)[2] /
          tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, abl$few_shot, mean)[1] - 1
tn <- tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, factor(abl$top_n, levels = sort(unique(abl$top_n))), mean)
ti <- tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$tissue, mean)
delta <- mean(merge(
  aggregate(hit_at_5 ~ dataset, llm, mean),
  ora[, c("dataset", "hit_at_5")], by = "dataset",
  suffixes = c("_llm", "_ora"))$hit_at_5_llm -
    merge(aggregate(hit_at_5 ~ dataset, llm, mean),
          ora[, c("dataset", "hit_at_5")], by = "dataset",
          suffixes = c("_llm", "_ora"))$hit_at_5_ora)
n_overlap <- nrow(merge(aggregate(hit_at_5 ~ dataset, llm, mean),
                        ora[, c("dataset", "hit_at_5")], by = "dataset"))
```

# Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are now routinely wrapped around differential
expression (DE) analysis, and the resulting mechanistic narratives are almost
always evaluated by whether they read plausibly. We argue that this evaluation
is unfalsifiable, and replace it with a benchmark built on perturbation
experiments whose mechanism is known independently of the transcriptome.
We present **DEGinsight**, an R package that turns a DE table into structured,
auditable mechanistic hypotheses, and a benchmark of `r N_DS` public
perturbation RNA-seq datasets spanning six drug–target axes (mTORC1,
glucocorticoid receptor, HDAC, BCR–ABL, TNFR1, TLR4) in six human cell systems.
For each dataset three mechanism components are frozen before any model is
called, and every interpretation is scored on mechanism recovery, on a
hallucination rate computed against the controlled vocabulary, and on measured
token cost.

The most important result is a null model. Over-representation analysis (ORA)
alone places a canonical pathway in the top five for `r ora5n`/`r N_DS`
datasets (`r f2(ora5)`) and in the top ten for `r ora10n`/`r N_DS`
(`r f2(ora10)`). Because the enrichment table is exactly what the model is
given as input, the honest question is not whether a model can name the
pathway — it usually can, because the pathway was already there — but what it
adds beyond the table. On the datasets where both arms are complete, LLM
pathway recall did not exceed the ORA control
(preliminary: Δ = `r sprintf("%+.2f", delta)`, n = `r n_overlap`), while component-level
recovery — the part ORA cannot express — reached
`r f2(rec_min)`–`r f2(rec_max)` at a median cost of
$`r sprintf("%.4f", cost_med)` per dataset with a
`r pct(hal_max)` measured hallucination rate under schema constraint and
post-hoc term auditing. A 48-cell ablation of prompt design contradicts
standard practice in two directions: few-shot exemplars *reduce* recovery
from `r f2(fs_off)` to `r f2(fs_on)` while increasing prompt tokens by
`r pct(fs_tok)`, and widening the enrichment table from 10 to 30 pathways is
worth more than any instruction we tried. We release the package, the frozen
ground truth and the full benchmark so that claims about LLM-assisted
interpretation can be stated as differences against a stated control.

# 1. Introduction

A differential expression analysis ends with a table, and the table is not a
result. The step that turns gene lists into mechanism — which pathway is
causal, which is a passenger, what the direction implies, what experiment
would settle it — is still done by hand, in prose, by whoever wrote the paper.
It is the slowest and least reproducible part of a transcriptomics workflow,
and it is exactly the part that LLMs are good at: they have read the
literature, they can hold twenty pathways in view at once, and they produce
fluent mechanistic text.

The consequence is a rapidly growing literature of "LLM interprets your
RNA-seq" tools, and a much smaller literature on whether those interpretations
are correct. The dominant evaluation is plausibility: show a domain expert the
output and ask whether it is reasonable. This cannot detect the failure mode
that matters. A model that has memorized that rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 will
write a convincing mTOR story from *any* macrophage dataset; an expert reading
the output will find nothing wrong with it, because nothing is wrong with it
as prose. The question is whether the evidence in the data supports it.

Two things are needed to make this testable. First, datasets whose mechanism
is known independently of the transcriptome — perturbation experiments, where
the drug's target or the knockout is the answer key. Second, a null model that
says how much of the answer is already visible in the input the model is
handed. The second is usually missing, and its absence inflates every claim in
the field: if the enrichment table places the correct pathway at rank 1, then
a model that copies rank 1 "recovers the mechanism" without adding anything.

We built DEGinsight to make both possible. The package takes a DE table,
computes enrichment against a bundled pathway collection, asks a model for
structured hypotheses under a schema that forbids inventing terms, then audits
the output mechanically — every cited pathway is checked against the input
table and the controlled vocabulary, and a violation rate is reported instead
of trusted. Because the audit is deterministic, the expensive part (the model
call) can be cached and the scoring can be recomputed for free.

We then benchmarked it on `r N_DS` perturbation datasets with pre-registered
mechanism ground truth, and asked four questions: (i) how much does plain ORA
already recover; (ii) does the model recover mechanism components at the level
of the known biology; (iii) does the audit hold, and at what cost; (iv) which
prompt-design choices actually help.

# 2. Package design

DEGinsight is a conventional R package (R ≥ 4.1) with no compiled code and
four dependencies; it is deliberately thin, because its job is to be the
auditable seam between an enrichment table and a language model, not to
re-implement enrichment.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat('
| Function | Role |
|---|---|
| `run_ora()` | hypergeometric ORA over a GMT collection, BH-adjusted |
| `build_interpretation_prompt()` | assembles the ontology-constrained prompt |
| `call_llm()` | one request, JSON mode when a schema is given, bounded retries |
| `validate_terms()` | post-hoc audit: citations vs input table vs vocabulary |
| `interpret_enrichment()` | the wrapper most users call |
| `interpret_ensemble()` | majority vote across models, with Jaccard agreement |
| `judge_mechanism()` | rubric-based recovery score from a *different* model |
| `estimate_cost()` | billed tokens × published prices |
')
```

Three design decisions matter for the benchmark.

**The schema is the guard, not the prompt.** `supporting_pathways` is typed as
an array of strings, and `validate_terms()` re-checks each returned term
against the input table and the vocabulary after generation. A model that
ignores the instruction is therefore counted, not silently trusted. The
reported hallucination rate is the output of this check.

**JSON mode is conditional.** DeepSeek-compatible endpoints reject a
schema-less JSON request and require the literal token "json" in the prompt;
`call_llm()` requests JSON only when a schema is supplied, and the prompt
builder emits the word. Without this, the call fails with HTTP 400 rather
than degrading quietly — a small detail that decides whether a pipeline is
usable inside a loop.

**Every call is cached by content hash** of prompt, model and temperature.
Re-scoring, re-rendering the report and trying a new metric cost nothing, and
a run becomes reproducible in the strong sense: the same inputs return the
same strings.

# 3. Benchmark design

## 3.1 Datasets

Six public RNA-seq perturbation experiments were selected for one property:
the mechanism is known from the perturbation itself, not inferred from the
expression data.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Dataset = gt$dataset_id,
             GEO = gt$gse,
             Perturbation = gt$perturbagen,
             System = gt$cell_type),
  caption = "Benchmark datasets. The series accessions are public; DE tables and cached model responses are in the repository.")
```

```{r, results='asis'}
cat("**Pre-registered mechanism components** (frozen before the first model call):\n\n")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(gt))) {
  comp <- gsub("\\|", "; ", gt$gt_components[i])
  cat("- **", gt$dataset_id[i], "** — ", comp, "\n", sep = "")
}
cat("\nThe `gt_components` column was committed to version control before any\n")
cat("model was called and was not edited afterwards.\n")
```

The six cover distinct target classes: an kinase inhibitor of a fusion
oncoprotein (imatinib/BCR–ABL), a steroid receptor agonist (dexamethasone/GR),
an epigenetic modifier (vorinostat/HDAC), an immunomodulatory drug
(rapamycin/mTORC1), and two receptor-level inflammatory stimuli (TNF-α/TNFR1,
LPS/TLR4). Four of six are primary or stem-cell-derived human systems rather
than immortalized lines, which is where an LLM's priors are least likely to
have memorized a specific dataset.

## 3.2 Differential expression

Series-matrix or supplementary count data were processed to gene-level tables
with limma, falling back to a Welch *t*-test when a design did not support a
linear model; Salmon quantifications were summed to gene level through
mygene.info annotation. One dataset (vorinostat) ships only as an xlsx
workbook and was parsed at the sheet-XML level.

An adaptive rule was fixed before scoring: if fewer than 20 genes pass
padj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1, the pipeline falls back to the 150 smallest
*p*-value genes balanced by direction, and records `deg_mode` in the output.
Two datasets required the fallback; one (rapamycin in NK cells) yields zero
genes at the strict threshold, which is a property of the experiment, not of
the pipeline.

```{r}
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(gt)), function(i) {
  f <- file.path("../benchmark/deg_tables", paste0(gt$dataset_id[i], ".rds"))
  o <- readRDS(f); d <- o$deg
  sig <- !is.na(d$padj) & !is.na(d$log2FoldChange) &
    d$padj < 0.05 & abs(d$log2FoldChange) > 1
  data.frame(Dataset = gt$dataset_id[i], Genes = nrow(d),
             DEG = sum(sig, na.rm = TRUE),
             Up = sum(sig & d$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             Down = sum(sig & d$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             Samples = paste0(length(o$treat_samples), " vs ",
                              length(o$ctrl_samples)),
             Mode = if (sum(sig, na.rm = TRUE) >= 20) "strict" else "top-150")
})
deg_tab <- do.call(rbind, rows)
knitr::kable(deg_tab, caption = "DE yield per dataset (padj < 0.05, |log2FC| > 1) and the DEG-selection mode actually used.")
```

## 3.3 Ground truth and the projection problem

Mechanism ground truth is text, and text is not directly comparable, so we
used two scorings with different failure modes.

*Component recovery* is a synonym-aware keyword score: each pre-registered
component carries a list of acceptable surface forms
(e.g. `mTORC1 inhibition|mTOR inhibition` and
`translational suppression/ribosomal/ribosome/protein synthesis/anabolic`),
the full interpretation is Unicode-normalised (so NF-κB and NF-kB compare
equal) and the fraction of components with at least one hit is reported. It is
free, deterministic and reproducible, and it is deliberately generous: it
rewards a correct idea expressed in unexpected words.

*Judge recovery* uses a second model with a strict rubric, always a different
model from the one being scored (cross-judging), which removes self-preference
bias without needing a third vendor.

For pathway-level comparison against ORA, the ground truth must be projected
onto the same vocabulary the enrichment tool uses. We map each dataset onto
its canonical Hallmark representatives *a priori* (`expected_gmt` in
`ground_truth.csv`). The mapping is one annotator's judgement and is therefore
the weakest link in the absolute numbers — but because the **same** projection
is applied to the ORA arm and the LLM arm, it cancels out of the comparison
that the paper is actually about.

## 3.4 The ORA-only control

The control is the benchmark's load-bearing element. The ORA table is the
model's input; if the correct pathway sits at rank 1 of that table, a model
that restates it has demonstrated nothing. We therefore score the top-*k* ORA
terms as if they were an interpretation, against the same ground truth, and
report hit@5 and hit@10 alongside every model number.

# 4. Results

## 4.1 Plain enrichment already recovers the canonical pathway

```{r fig.height=2.9}
pal <- c(ORA_only = "grey40", LLM = "#1f6fb4")
recall$arm <- factor(recall$arm, levels = c("ORA_only", "LLM"),
                     labels = c("ORA table only", "LLM interpretation"))
ggplot(recall, aes(reorder(dataset, hit_at_5), hit_at_5, fill = arm)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey40", "#1f6fb4"), name = NULL) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "canonical pathway in top-5 (0/1)",
       title = "ORA alone is a strong baseline")
```

Across all `r N_DS` datasets the ORA table alone puts a canonical pathway in
the top five for `r ora5n` datasets (`r f2(ora5)`) and in the top ten for
`r ora10n` (`r f2(ora10)`). The two misses are informative rather than
random: in vorinostat-treated A498 cells the first canonical hit is at rank 35
— HDAC inhibition produces a cell-cycle collapse whose Hallmark signature is
dominated by E2F targets, and the enrichment table reflects that — and in
imatinib-treated K562 cells the first hit is at rank 9, behind the same
proliferation signature.

This is the single most consequential number in the paper, because it sets the
bar for every claim in this space. A tool that reports "the model correctly
identified mTORC1 signalling" on a dataset where mTORC1 signalling is rank 1 of
the input table has measured its own enrichment step.

## 4.2 What the model adds, and what it does not

On the datasets where both arms are complete (n = `r n_overlap`), pathway-level
recall of the LLM output did not exceed the ORA control
(mean Δ = `r sprintf("%+.2f", delta)`). We report this as a result rather than
a failure: the model is not a better pathway finder than a hypergeometric
test, and there is no reason it should be, since it is reading the test's
output.

What it does add is the layer the test cannot produce. Component-level
recovery over completed runs ranged from `r f2(rec_min)` to `r f2(rec_max)`
(mean `r f2(rec_mean)`), driven by mechanism statements that no enrichment
term contains — for example, that rapamycin's transcriptional footprint in NK
cells is a hypoxia/glycolytic shift secondary to mTORC1 loss rather than
direct translational control, or that dexamethasone's effect in airway
organoids is GR-driven repression of an NF-κB inflammatory module.

```{r}
agg <- aggregate(cbind(recovery_keyword, hallucination_rate, cost_usd,
                       completion_tokens) ~ model, bench, mean,
                 na.rm = TRUE, na.action = na.pass)
agg$n_runs <- as.vector(table(bench$model)[agg$model])
agg <- agg[order(-agg$recovery_keyword), c("model", "n_runs", "recovery_keyword",
                                           "hallucination_rate", "cost_usd",
                                           "completion_tokens")]
knitr::kable(agg, digits = 4,
  caption = "Per-model means over completed runs. n_runs is reported because a mean over one run is an observation, not an estimate.")
```

## 4.3 Hallucination is an audit result, not a model property

The measured hallucination rate is `r pct(hal_max)` in every completed run.
This number should be read carefully: it is the output of
`validate_terms()`, which checks every cited pathway against the input table
and the controlled vocabulary, so a zero means the guard held — the schema
constrained generation and the audit caught anything that escaped. It is not
evidence that the model would be accurate without the guard, and the ablation
shows the guard is doing work: prompt variants that widen the table's
influence also change what the model cites.

## 4.4 Prompt design: two results that contradict standard practice

```{r fig.height=2.8}
a <- aggregate(recovery_keyword ~ top_n + few_shot + tissue, abl, mean)
a$few_shot <- factor(a$few_shot, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                     labels = c("no exemplar", "few-shot"))
ggplot(a, aes(factor(top_n), recovery_keyword, colour = few_shot,
              group = few_shot, shape = few_shot)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ tissue, labeller = as_labeller(
    c(`FALSE` = "no tissue context", `TRUE` = "with tissue context"))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey35", "#c0504d"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "pathways shown to the model (top_n)", y = "mean component recovery",
       title = "Ablation over 48 prompt configurations")
```

The ablation grid varies three things a user actually controls — a few-shot
exemplar (on/off), the number of pathways shown (5/10/20/30) and tissue
context (on/off) — over three datasets at a fixed reference model, 48
configurations.

**Few-shot prompting hurts.** Mean component recovery falls from
`r f2(fs_off)` without an exemplar to `r f2(fs_on)` with one, while prompt
tokens rise by `r pct(fs_tok)`. The mechanism is visible in the outputs: the
model reproduces the *shape* of the demonstration — same number of
hypotheses, same rhetorical structure, often the same pathway family — instead
of the evidence in front of it. Few-shot is the default recommendation for
structured output, and for this task it is a loss on both accuracy and cost.

**Wider context is better.** Recovery rises from `r f2(tn[["10"]])` at
`top_n = 10` to `r f2(tn[["30"]])` at `top_n = 30`, monotonically apart from a
dip at 10. The display convention of showing the "top five significant hits"
is exactly wrong here: truncating the table removes the alternatives the model
needs in order to judge which term is causal and which is a passenger.

**Tissue context is nearly neutral** (`r f2(ti[["FALSE"]])` absent vs
`r f2(ti[["TRUE"]])` present) — cheap enough to keep, but not a lever.

## 4.5 Where it fails

Three failure modes recur and are worth stating because they are invisible to
plausibility-based evaluation:

- *Direction inversion under weak contrasts.* When the DEG list comes from the
  top-150 fallback, the model frequently names the right pathway with the
  wrong sign. The current component metric is direction-agnostic, so this is
  under-penalised — a limitation of the metric, and the first thing we would
  fix.
- *Passenger promotion.* In imatinib-treated K562 cells, cell-cycle shutdown
  dominates the DE list, and the model sometimes ranks proliferation terms
  above the BCR–ABL/JAK–STAT axis that caused them. ORA cannot distinguish a
  target from its consequence; the model often can, and when it cannot, the
  ranking is where it shows.
- *Fluency without commitment.* Hypotheses graded "moderate" tend to hedge in
  a way that is neither wrong nor testable ("may reflect a shift in…"). The
  `follow_up_experiment` field was added specifically to force a falsifiable
  statement, and it is the field most often left generic.

# 5. Discussion

The finding that plain ORA matches an LLM on pathway naming is not an argument
against LLM assistance; it is an argument about what to measure. Enrichment
analysis answers "which annotated sets are over-represented"; a bench
scientist reading the same table asks "so what". The gap between those two
questions is where the model earns its cost, and it is a gap that
pathway-recall metrics cannot see.

Three practical consequences follow.

First, **report an ORA control**. Any evaluation of LLM-assisted
enrichment interpretation that does not state how much of the answer is in the
input table is uninterpretable, in the same way a classifier accuracy without a
majority-class baseline is uninterpretable. The control is free and takes one
extra column of scoring code.

Second, **prefer defaults that look wrong**. Two of the three prompt knobs we
tested behave opposite to convention: exemplars hurt, and the wider table
helps. Both are consistent with a single explanation — the model does better
when it is reasoning over the data and worse when it is pattern-matching a
template — and both are cheap to adopt.

Third, **make the guard mechanical**. The zero hallucination rate in this
benchmark is a property of `validate_terms()`, not of the model. A pipeline
that reports a hallucination rate it did not compute itself has no such
number.

The larger point concerns the direction of the field. Agents that *design*
perturbation experiments now exist and are evaluated against held-out screens
[12]; the natural next step is not a better narrative generator but a closed
loop in which a proposed mechanism is converted into a discriminating
experiment and the model is scored on whether the experiment resolved the
ambiguity. DEGinsight's `follow_up_experiment` field is a placeholder for
that loop, not an end in itself.

# 6. Limitations

- **Partial model grid.** `r N_DONE` of `r N_CELLS` planned dataset–model
  cells are complete. Per-model means over one or two runs are observations,
  not estimates, and the model comparison is within a single vendor; whether
  the prompt-design findings transfer across vendors is untested.
- **Coarse ground truth.** Three components per dataset detects gross failure
  but cannot separate a good interpretation from a very good one.
- **One annotator projection.** The Hallmark projection of the ground truth is
  a single expert's judgement. It cancels in the ORA-versus-LLM comparison but
  not in absolute recovery numbers.
- **Direction is under-scored.** Component matching ignores the sign of
  regulation, which we know lets direction inversions through.
- **No wet-lab validation.** Every proposed follow-up experiment is a
  proposal; none was performed.

# 7. Methods

**Data acquisition.** GEO series matrices and supplementary files were
downloaded with size-pinned resumable transfers. Where a study provided raw
Salmon quantifications, transcript-level effective counts were summed to gene
level using mygene.info symbols restricted to one-to-one mappings.

**Differential expression.** limma with eBayes on log-CPM values; Welch
*t*-test with BH correction where a design matrix was not estimable. One
study's counts were supplied as an xlsx workbook and read at the sheet-XML
level to avoid loading the whole workbook.

**Enrichment.** One-sided hypergeometric test against 49 Hallmark-style
pathway sets, BH-adjusted; terms with fewer than 5 overlapping genes dropped.
`top_n` controls how many terms enter the prompt (default 20).

**Prompt.** The model receives the contrast in words, the species, the tissue,
and a table of pathways with overlap counts, gene symbols and adjusted
*p*-values, plus a schema requiring named hypotheses with supporting pathways
drawn only from that table, driver genes from the input, an evidence grade and
a discriminating follow-up experiment. Temperature 0.

**Audit.** Each cited pathway is normalised and checked against (i) the input
table and (ii) the controlled vocabulary; the fraction failing both is the
hallucination rate.

**Scoring.** Component recovery and cross-model judging as described in
§3.3. Judge prompts were identical across runs; the judge was never the model
under evaluation.

**Cost.** Prompt and completion tokens as reported by the provider, multiplied
by published per-million prices at the time of the run
(`benchmark/models.csv` records both, so the accounting can be recomputed).

# 8. Availability

The package (MIT), the frozen ground truth, the DE tables, every cached model
response and the scripts that regenerate all figures in this manuscript are at
https://github.com/omixcore/DEGinsight. The benchmark runs end-to-end with
`Rscript benchmark/02_run_benchmark.R` given an API key; scoring, the ORA
control and this document require no key.
